23.title: Relative Value & Comps: Positioning Auto ABS
23.prerequisite: Know how WAL, credit enhancement, triggers, pay rules, and issuer quality shape an Auto ABS bond.
23.later: This comparison framework feeds Day 25's trading watchlist and Day 26's capstone price talk.

sections.label: Build
sections.title: Build a fair comp set
sections.lead: A useful comp set matches the risks that determine both cash-flow timing and investor confidence.

bullets.title: Issuer tier
bullets.text: Repeat issuers with strong operations and clean data often earn better liquidity and tighter spreads.

bullets.title: Structure
bullets.text: Compare subordination, OC, reserve, pro-rata windows, flip conditions, and PDL mechanics.

bullets.title: Tenor
bullets.text: Match base and stressed WAL before comparing spreads so time risk is normalized.

bullets.title: Liquidity
bullets.text: Deal size, benchmark status, and on-the-run presence can move spreads even when credit is similar.

sections.callout: A spread comparison without a WAL comparison is usually an apples-to-oranges comparison.

sections.label: Frame
sections.title: Place Auto ABS beside its peers
sections.lead: Prime, subprime, card ABS, and CLOs provide context, but they do not carry identical collateral or structural risks.

bullets.title: Prime vs subprime
bullets.text: Subprime seniors usually trade wider because expected losses and severity are higher and OC may build more slowly.

bullets.title: Cards
bullets.text: Card ABS often has shorter WAL, revolving collateral, and early-amortization events, so its senior spread is not a direct Auto ABS substitute.

bullets.title: CLOs
bullets.text: CLOs hold corporate loans and have a different liability stack; use them mainly as a signal of broader risk appetite.

sections.callout: Adjacent asset classes are a market-temperature check, not a shortcut around deal-level analysis.

sections.label: Measure
sections.title: Use quick relative-value metrics
sections.lead: A few simple measures make a pricing opinion transparent enough for a team to challenge.

bullets.title: Spread per WAL
bullets.text: Divide spread in basis points by WAL in years for a rough measure of carry per year of exposure.

bullets.title: Margin of safety
bullets.text: Compare available CE to required stressed CE; a ratio above 1.0 suggests cushion, subject to timing.

bullets.title: Extension score
bullets.text: Add one flag each for long pro-rata, weak flips, thin XS versus fees, and optional advances.

bullets.title: OC path
bullets.text: Faster expected OC build from sequential pay and strict trapping supports tighter pricing.

sections.callout: An extension score of 2 or more is a practical reason to demand roughly 10–20 bps more spread.

sections.label: Decide
sections.title: Lab: Set the talk
sections.lead: A prime AAA comp prints at T+112 with 2.7-year WAL, strict flips, daily sweeps, and 12% OC; your 2.6-year deal matches those protections and adds 25 bps of reserve.

bullets.title: Decision
bullets.text: Propose T+108–110 because tenor and core structure match while the larger reserve adds protection.

bullets.title: Extension check
bullets.text: Score long pro-rata, weak flips, thin XS, and optional advances from 0–4; at 2 or more, widen talk by 10–20 bps.

bullets.title: Challenge
bullets.text: Write the single secondary-market observation that would move your view by plus or minus 10 bps.

sections.callout: Your output: talk spread, extension score, and one sentence connecting both to the comp.

flashcards.front: Why match WAL when comparing spreads?
flashcards.back: It normalizes time and extension exposure, making the spread comparison more meaningful.

flashcards.front: What is spread/WAL?
flashcards.back: Spread in bps divided by WAL in years—a rough carry-per-year measure.

flashcards.front: What does a margin-of-safety ratio above 1.0 suggest?
flashcards.back: Available CE exceeds required stressed CE, although timing and pay rules still matter.

flashcards.front: Name two extension flags.
flashcards.back: A long pro-rata window and optional advances; weak flips and thin XS are two others.

flashcards.front: Why might a repeat issuer trade tighter?
flashcards.back: Investors may value its operating record, data quality, familiarity, and secondary liquidity.

quiz.q: Which comparison is most defensible?
quiz.explain: WAL matching normalizes time risk, while structural adjustments capture the remaining differences.

quiz.q: Which feature should normally tighten senior spreads?
quiz.explain: A strict early flip accelerates senior amortization and reduces extension risk.

quiz.q: Why do subprime seniors usually trade wider than prime seniors?
options: They carry higher expected CNL and severity
quiz.explain: Higher expected loss and severity raise risk even when the senior rating is similar.

quiz.q: An extension flag score rises from 1 to 3. What is the likely pricing response?
quiz.explain: More extension flags mean investors should demand more compensation.

quiz.q: What is the best role for CLO spreads in an Auto ABS analysis?
quiz.explain: CLO collateral and structures differ, but their spreads can indicate the market's general appetite for risk.

24.title: ESG, EVs & Future Trends in Auto ABS
24.prerequisite: Understand recoveries, severity, OC, reserves, triggers, and sequential versus pro-rata pay.
24.later: These EV and governance questions become risk-and-mitigant inputs in the Day 26 capstone and future pool monitoring.

sections.label: Lens
sections.title: Make ESG operational
sections.lead: In Auto ABS, ESG becomes useful when it changes diligence questions, data quality, or servicing controls.

bullets.title: Governance
bullets.text: Review reporting timeliness, servicing standards, complaint handling, repossession practices, and privacy controls.

bullets.title: Social
bullets.text: Examine hardship, extension, and deferral practices plus fair treatment across origination and servicing channels.

bullets.title: Environmental
bullets.text: Track ICE, hybrid, and EV mix alongside indirect emissions and recycling or disposal considerations.

bullets.title: Disclosure
bullets.text: Consistent static pools and accurate trustee reporting are often the most decision-useful governance evidence.

sections.callout: The strongest ESG question is often: what data or control would reveal the risk early?

sections.label: Diagnose
sections.title: Trace EV risk into recoveries
sections.lead: An EV loan can follow the same default path as an ICE loan yet produce a different net loss because resale economics differ.

bullets.title: Battery economics
bullets.text: Battery health, rapid depreciation, and costly repairs can reduce auction proceeds.

bullets.title: Obsolescence
bullets.text: Fast model-year changes and software-locked features can weaken used-vehicle demand.

bullets.title: Repair network
bullets.text: Parts and service availability affect both time to sale and net recovery.

bullets.title: Severity
bullets.text: Lower recoveries at the same defaults produce higher net loss severity.

sections.callout: EV exposure is primarily a recovery and severity question—not automatically a default-rate conclusion.

sections.label: Protect
sections.title: Match mitigants to the risk
sections.lead: EV-heavy pools can offset uncertain resale outcomes through stronger protection and better remarketing evidence.

bullets.title: More cushion
bullets.text: Higher OC targets or reserves provide protection when recovery uncertainty is elevated.

bullets.title: Faster de-risking
bullets.text: Strict 60+ and CNL flips plus stronger XS trapping accelerate senior paydown.

bullets.title: Better disposal
bullets.text: Specialized EV remarketing, warranties, and certified programs can support resale proceeds.

bullets.title: Better segmentation
bullets.text: Request EV share, battery-age proxies, and EV-versus-ICE recovery and severity data.

sections.callout: A mitigant is credible only when its benefit can be measured or contractually enforced.

sections.label: Scan
sections.title: Lab: Challenge an EV-heavy pool
sections.lead: Pool A is 35% EV and recent regional auctions show EV recoveries about 10 points below comparable ICE vehicles.

bullets.title: Data ask
bullets.text: Request EV-versus-ICE recoveries plus weighted-average battery age or health by model year.

bullets.title: Remarketing ask
bullets.text: Confirm specialist auction channels, repair networks, and warranty or certified-resale support.

bullets.title: Structure decision
bullets.text: Test an OC target 150 bps above an ICE-heavy deal, a reserve 50 bps larger, and strict 60+/CNL flips.

bullets.title: Equity impact
bullets.text: Explain that higher targets and stronger trapping delay equity cash while seniors de-risk faster.

sections.callout: Your output: three diligence questions, two structural mitigants, and the equity-timing trade-off.

flashcards.front: Which ESG pillar covers reporting accuracy?
flashcards.back: Governance, because it concerns controls, transparency, and accountability.

flashcards.front: How can battery condition affect an ABS deal?
flashcards.back: Weaker battery health can reduce resale proceeds and raise loss severity.

flashcards.front: What is the fastest structural response to weaker recoveries?
flashcards.back: Flip earlier to sequential pay and trap excess spread to accelerate senior de-risking.

flashcards.front: Which EV stratification is especially useful?
flashcards.back: EV-versus-ICE recovery and severity data, supported by battery-age or health proxies.

flashcards.front: Why can subscription models matter?
flashcards.back: Different contract forms may change asset eligibility and how cash flows fit the waterfall.

quiz.q: Which EV feature most directly affects recovery severity?
quiz.explain: Battery depreciation can materially reduce resale value and therefore recoveries.

quiz.q: Which request best improves EV-specific analysis?
quiz.explain: Segmented recovery data isolates the risk that EV collateral may behave differently.

quiz.q: Reporting timeliness belongs primarily to which ESG pillar?
quiz.explain: Timely, accurate reporting is a governance and control issue.

quiz.q: What does higher OC do for an EV-heavy pool?
quiz.explain: OC does not prevent defaults, but it provides additional protection against loss uncertainty.

quiz.q: Which trend could require new eligibility and waterfall analysis?
quiz.explain: Subscription structures may produce cash flows and legal forms different from conventional retail loans.

25.title: Secondary Trading, Watchlists & Downgrades
25.prerequisite: Know the core performance KPIs, OC and IC tests, PDL mechanics, reserve behavior, and relative-value framework.
25.later: The watchlist thresholds become the monitoring plan in Day 26's capstone and the controls logic used in later modeling days.

sections.label: Read
sections.title: Decode the secondary market
sections.lead: Secondary levels reflect current credit information plus the market's willingness to make a two-way price.

bullets.title: Axes and BWICs
bullets.text: Dealer buy/sell interests and bids-wanted lists create observable prints and market color.

bullets.title: Liquidity tiers
bullets.text: Large on-the-run AAA bonds usually trade more easily than small mezzanine positions.

bullets.title: Bid-offer
bullets.text: The gap can widen during risk-off periods even when a deal's own KPIs remain stable.

bullets.title: Dispersion
bullets.text: Issuer tier and structural quality can separate spreads for bonds with the same WAL.

sections.callout: A wider bid-offer can be a market-liquidity signal, not proof that collateral suddenly worsened.

sections.label: Monitor
sections.title: Build an actionable watchlist
sections.lead: A useful watchlist pairs each performance signal with a defined escalation or trading action.

bullets.title: OC slope
bullets.text: Two months below target—or flat OC while delinquencies rise—deserves attention.

bullets.title: IC cushion
bullets.text: A senior IC ratio below roughly 1.02x warns that equity may shut off and PDL use may approach.

bullets.title: Delinquency
bullets.text: A 60+ rate above its amber threshold and still rising is an early deterioration cue.

bullets.title: Liquidity reserve
bullets.text: Repeated reserve draws without replenishment indicate cash-flow stress.

sections.callout: Do not write 'watch OC'; write the threshold, observation window, owner, and action.

sections.label: Anticipate
sections.title: Spot downgrade pressure early
sections.lead: Rating actions can come from performance, counterparties, methodology, or documentation—not just realized losses.

bullets.title: Mezz pressure
bullets.text: Prolonged equity shut-off, an outstanding PDL, and slow OC build increase downgrade risk.

bullets.title: Senior pressure
bullets.text: Prime seniors are more likely to face concern after structural erosion, documentation changes, or major methodology shifts.

bullets.title: Counterparties
bullets.text: Servicer or account-bank downgrades matter if required remedies are not completed on time.

bullets.title: Outlook first
bullets.text: Multiple amber months may lead to an outlook change before a formal downgrade.

sections.callout: A rating is an output; the watchlist should surface the inputs before the output changes.

sections.label: Act
sections.title: Lab: Call the watchlist status
sections.lead: OC moved 1.087x → 1.091x → 1.105x against a 1.10x target, while 60+ fell 2.4% → 2.2% → 2.0%; IC is 1.03x, no PDL is outstanding, and the reserve is full.

bullets.title: Status
bullets.text: Take the deal off watch only if the latest OC pass is confirmed and the improving delinquency trend persists.

bullets.title: Equity call
bullets.text: With OC above target and IC above 1.0x, equity is likely to resume next month if the documents require no extra cure period.

bullets.title: Spread call
bullets.text: The positive OC slope and falling 60+ rate support tighter spreads versus the last print, subject to market liquidity.

sections.callout: Your output: on/off watch, equity on/off, spread direction, and the exact threshold that would reverse the call.

flashcards.front: What is a BWIC?
flashcards.back: A bids-wanted-in-competition process used to solicit secondary bids and establish market color.

flashcards.front: What does IC below 1.0x usually do to equity?
flashcards.back: It shuts equity distributions off and redirects cash to protect the notes.

flashcards.front: Name two mezzanine downgrade cues.
flashcards.back: A prolonged equity shut-off and an outstanding PDL; slow OC build is another.

flashcards.front: What signals a convincing cure?
flashcards.back: Triggers pass for multiple months, OC trends upward, and delinquencies trend down.

flashcards.front: Why can a stable bond still have a wider bid-offer?
flashcards.back: Sector risk-off conditions, dealer balance-sheet limits, or a BWIC overhang can reduce liquidity.

quiz.q: Which combination most strongly supports buying on cure?
options: OC rising and 60+ falling for several months
quiz.explain: A sustained improving OC path and declining delinquencies indicate that the structure is curing.

quiz.q: What should happen when IC falls below 1.0x?
options: The reserve is paid to equity
quiz.explain: Cash is diverted away from equity to protect senior obligations.

quiz.q: Which can widen bid-offer despite stable deal performance?
quiz.explain: Liquidity withdrawal can affect pricing independently of the deal's underlying KPIs.

quiz.q: Which issue is most relevant to a senior outlook change?
quiz.explain: Reduced structural protection can weaken senior resilience and alter rating-agency conclusions.

quiz.q: What makes a watchlist threshold useful?
options: It has a metric, observation window, and action
quiz.explain: A defined threshold and response turns monitoring into a repeatable decision process.

26.title: Grand Capstone: End-to-End Auto ABS Case
26.prerequisite: Bring together presale reading, collateral stratification, waterfall modeling, stress testing, pricing comps, and surveillance KPIs.
26.later: The capstone becomes the baseline case you refine with ratings backsolves, structuring choices, Excel controls, and funding operations in Days 27–32.

sections.label: Assemble
sections.title: Collect decision-grade inputs
sections.lead: The capstone starts by reconciling the legal structure, collateral profile, and economic environment.

bullets.title: Presale
bullets.text: Capture classes, CE, OC and IC tests, delinquency and CNL triggers, pay rules, and PDL language.

bullets.title: Collateral
bullets.text: Summarize FICO, LTV, term, new/used mix, and dealer or geographic concentrations.

bullets.title: Macro
bullets.text: Use unemployment, rates, and used-car values to shape severity, prepay, and roll-rate assumptions.

bullets.title: Consistency
bullets.text: Make sure every model assumption has a source or is clearly labeled as judgment.

sections.callout: A polished output cannot rescue inputs that contradict the presale or collateral tape.

sections.label: Model
sections.title: Run six periods, twice
sections.lead: The base case demonstrates normal mechanics, while the stress case tests trapping, flips, cures, and extension.

bullets.title: Base
bullets.text: Keep triggers passing after reserve top-up and allow equity while targets remain satisfied.

bullets.title: Stress
bullets.text: Raise roll rates, severity, and fees; lower prepays; force an early OC fail and test whether it cures by Period 4.

bullets.title: Track
bullets.text: Record XS, reserve change, equity, A and B principal, OC end and ratio proxy, plus PDL if implemented.

bullets.title: Compare
bullets.text: Explain the equity-off timeline, cure month, and change in senior WAL proxy.

sections.callout: A credible stress tells a cash-flow story period by period—not just a larger loss number.

sections.label: Recommend
sections.title: Write the investor one-pager
sections.lead: The memo should let a decision-maker understand the deal, downside, and price view in minutes.

bullets.title: Snapshot
bullets.text: Name the issuer and series, closing date, collateral mix, class stack, and starting protection.

bullets.title: Mechanics
bullets.text: Show pay rules, key triggers, base-versus-stress OC paths, and equity on/off periods.

bullets.title: Risks
bullets.text: Pair three to five material risks with specific structural or operational mitigants.

bullets.title: Pricing
bullets.text: Give WAL-matched talk for A and B and show the comp-based rationale.

sections.callout: If a risk does not change your model, monitoring plan, or price, explain why it still belongs.

sections.label: Defend
sections.title: Lab: Defend the investment case
sections.kicker: One page, six periods, one decision
sections.lead: Build base and stress cases in which equity is off in P1–P2, OC cures by P3–P4 if plausible, and the Class A WAL proxy extends under stress.

bullets.title: Model output
bullets.text: Report equity on/off by period, OC cure month, and the change in A's WAL proxy from base to stress.

bullets.title: Price output
bullets.text: Propose talk for A and B; T+110/T+270 is an illustrative starting point when strict flips and daily sweeps support the structure.

bullets.title: Monitor
bullets.text: Escalate immediately if 60+ breaches amber while OC remains flat or declining for two periods.

bullets.title: Sensitivity
bullets.text: Estimate a 40 bps market move with ΔPrice ≈ −WAL × ΔYield × Price.

sections.callout: Your output: a reproducible one-pager whose model, price talk, and monitoring actions tell the same story.

flashcards.front: What are the three capstone evidence streams?
flashcards.back: Deal documents, collateral/tape data, and macro assumptions.

flashcards.front: What should an early OC fail do?
flashcards.back: Turn equity off, trap excess spread, and direct principal sequentially to accelerate cure.

flashcards.front: Which outputs compare base and stress?
flashcards.back: OC path, equity timeline, senior paydown or WAL proxy, reserve use, and any PDL path.

flashcards.front: What is the rough price-change formula?
flashcards.back: ΔPrice ≈ −WAL × ΔYield × Price.

flashcards.front: What makes a monitoring plan actionable?
flashcards.back: Each KPI has green/amber/red thresholds and a defined action on breach.

quiz.q: Which stress combination most plausibly extends Class A?
options: Faster prepays and early sequential pay
quiz.explain: Slower prepays and a delayed sequential flip keep senior principal outstanding longer.

quiz.q: What should a capstone model show after an OC fail?
options: XS is trapped and equity turns off
quiz.explain: The structure redirects cash away from equity to rebuild protection.

quiz.q: Which comp features deserve the greatest weight in price talk?
options: WAL plus flip and OC terms
quiz.explain: WAL and structural protection are central to exposure and downside behavior.

quiz.q: Which threshold should trigger an immediate pricing review?
options: 60+ above amber while OC is flat or falling
quiz.explain: Deteriorating delinquencies plus weak OC build directly challenge the original risk and extension view.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the one-pager?
options: Present a traceable investment decision concisely
quiz.explain: It summarizes the evidence and recommendation without pretending to replace source documents.

27.title: Ratings Methodology & CE Backsolve
27.prerequisite: Understand expected CNL, severity, subordination, OC, XS, reserves, triggers, and loss timing.
27.later: The CE backsolve provides the constraints for Day 28's structuring lab and the checks embedded in Day 29's model.

sections.label: Translate
sections.title: Follow the agency logic
sections.lead: A ratings analysis converts expected performance into stressed loss paths, then tests the actual waterfall against them.

bullets.title: Baseline
bullets.text: Begin with expected CNL and severity informed by static pools and vintages.

bullets.title: Stress
bullets.text: Apply rating-level multiples or curves to create AAA, A, and BBB loss paths and timing.

bullets.title: Overlay
bullets.text: Run those paths through pay rules, triggers, reserves, OC behavior, and PDL mechanics.

bullets.title: Test
bullets.text: Ask whether interest is timely and principal is fully paid by legal maturity under the relevant stress.

sections.callout: A rating is a stressed cash-flow survival conclusion, not simply a multiple applied to expected loss.

sections.label: Count
sections.title: Separate durable CE from conditional CE
sections.lead: Available protection combines funded, structural, and future cash-flow sources with different reliability.

bullets.title: Subordination
bullets.text: Junior notes and equity absorb losses first and generally provide the most durable protection.

bullets.title: OC
bullets.text: Assets in excess of notes provide funded cushion and can grow through sequential pay and trapping.

bullets.title: XS
bullets.text: Projected excess spread may receive a large haircut—or no credit—if it is not trapped or disappears under stress.

bullets.title: Reserve
bullets.text: A funded reserve covers shortfalls and is usually replenished before equity receives cash.

sections.callout: Headline CE overstates comfort when it treats uncertain future XS like funded subordination.

sections.label: Backsolve
sections.title: Compare required and available CE
sections.lead: A quick backsolve establishes whether the structure has enough nominal cushion before a full cash-flow test.

bullets.title: Required
bullets.text: Approximate stressed CNL by applying the relevant rating multiple to base CNL, then add timing cushion.

bullets.title: Available
bullets.text: Sum subordination to the class, OC, reserve, and only the haircutted XS expected to be trapped.

bullets.title: Margin
bullets.text: Compare available CE with required CE to identify surplus, deficit, or a thin borderline case.

bullets.title: Example
bullets.text: A 4% base CNL at 3× implies about 12% stressed CNL before timing considerations.

sections.callout: A 39% headline CE stack may look ample, but its quality still depends on pay rules and when losses arrive.

sections.label: Challenge
sections.title: Lab: Backsolve two rating levels
sections.lead: Base CNL is 3.5%. Use a 3× AAA stress and a 1.8× A stress, then compare them with the stated protection.

bullets.title: AAA result
bullets.text: 3.5% × 3 = 10.5% stressed CNL; 20% sub to A + 4% OC + 1% reserve gives 25% headline CE before timing.

bullets.title: AAA judgment
bullets.text: Headline CE is ample, but a long pro-rata window or front-loaded losses could still jeopardize timely senior payment.

bullets.title: A result
bullets.text: 3.5% × 1.8 = 6.3%; 8% equity plus 2% OC gives Class B 10% headline protection.

bullets.title: A judgment
bullets.text: The 10% headline amount exceeds 6.3%, but XS haircuts, severity timing, and the actual waterfall still require testing.

sections.callout: Your output: both calculations, an adequacy call, and two timing features that could overturn the headline result.

flashcards.front: What is the most durable CE component?
flashcards.back: Subordination, because junior claims absorb losses before the senior class.

flashcards.front: Why might an agency give XS zero credit?
flashcards.back: It may disappear under stress or may not be contractually trapped for noteholder protection.

flashcards.front: How do you estimate stressed CNL quickly?
flashcards.back: Multiply base CNL by the rating-level stress multiple, then consider timing cushion.

flashcards.front: Why can pro-rata pay raise required CE?
flashcards.back: It slows senior amortization and OC build, leaving the class exposed longer.

flashcards.front: What is available CE to a class?
flashcards.back: Subordination beneath it plus OC, reserve, and eligible haircutted trapped XS.

quiz.q: Base CNL is 3.5% and the AAA multiple is 3×. What is the quick stressed CNL?
quiz.explain: 3.5% multiplied by 3 equals 10.5%, before adding timing considerations.

quiz.q: Which CE source is most likely to receive a haircut?
quiz.explain: XS is a future cash flow that can shrink or vanish under stress.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of headline CE sums?
options: They can ignore loss timing and pay rules
quiz.explain: A sufficient lifetime total may still be unavailable when an early shortfall occurs.

quiz.q: Which change most increases senior timing risk?
quiz.explain: A longer pro-rata period keeps senior balances outstanding and slows protection build.

quiz.q: What does the agency ultimately test?
options: Timely interest and ultimate principal under stress
quiz.explain: The rating addresses contractual payment performance under the applicable stressed scenario.

28.title: Structuring Lab: Tune CE, Triggers, and Pay Rules
28.prerequisite: Know how required CE is backsolved and how OC, reserves, XS, flips, PDL, and cash control protect the notes.
28.later: The chosen blueprint becomes a formula-driven waterfall in Day 29 and a practical funding constraint in Days 31–32.

sections.label: Survey
sections.title: Know the lever board
sections.lead: Structuring is the job of combining loss protection, liquidity, timing controls, and issuer economics.

bullets.title: Subordination
bullets.text: Strong funded protection, but it raises weighted funding cost and reduces equity economics.

bullets.title: OC and reserve
bullets.text: OC builds loss cushion; the reserve stabilizes near-term interest and fee liquidity.

bullets.title: Pay rules
bullets.text: Short pro-rata windows, strict flips, and step-ups reduce extension by accelerating seniors.

bullets.title: PDL and controls
bullets.text: PDL permission protects senior interest, while lockboxes and frequent sweeps reduce commingling risk.

sections.callout: The 'best' structure depends on whose objective you are optimizing: rating, investor, or issuer.

sections.label: Optimize
sections.title: Use smart timing to reduce headline CE
sections.lead: Strict triggers and early sequential pay can make the same nominal CE more effective under stress.

bullets.title: Tight flips
bullets.text: OC, IC, delinquency, and CNL breaches trap cash before deterioration becomes severe.

bullets.title: Sequential bias
bullets.text: Earlier senior paydown builds OC faster and shifts timing risk toward equity.

bullets.title: Reserve over XS
bullets.text: A modestly larger funded reserve can reduce reliance on uncertain projected XS.

bullets.title: Trade-off
bullets.text: Less headline CE may be plausible only if the timing protections are enforceable and robust.

sections.callout: Smart timing does not eliminate credit risk; it reallocates when cash and protection become available.

sections.label: Compare
sections.title: Choose between two blueprints
sections.lead: Two structures can target the same rating while offering different spread and equity-timing outcomes.

bullets.title: Conservative
bullets.text: Use roughly 28–32% sub to A, 12% OC, a 1.5% reserve, tight pro-rata tests, a 24-month step-up, PDL, and daily sweeps.

bullets.title: Par-efficient
bullets.text: Use roughly 20–24% sub to A, 8–9% OC, a 0.75–1.0% reserve, milder pro-rata conditions, limited PDL, and weekly sweeps.

bullets.title: Investor outcome
bullets.text: The conservative design should de-risk seniors faster and support tighter AAA levels.

bullets.title: Issuer outcome
bullets.text: The par-efficient design preserves economics but may need a spread concession for extension risk.

sections.callout: Equal ratings do not mean equal cash-flow timing or equal relative value.

sections.label: Tune
sections.title: Lab: Design two structures
sections.lead: For Prime Auto 2025-A, build a conservative and a par-efficient structure, then force a three-period pro-rata-to-sequential flip.

bullets.title: Conservative case
bullets.text: Specify sub to A, 12% OC, 1.5% reserve, tight pro-rata tests, 24-month step-up, PDL, and daily sweeps.

bullets.title: Efficient case
bullets.text: Specify 8–9% OC, a 0.75–1.0% reserve, milder pro-rata tests, limited PDL, and weekly sweeps.

bullets.title: Model result
bullets.text: Compare each case's three-period OC path and equity on/off sequence after the flip.

bullets.title: 10 bps challenge
bullets.text: To tighten AAA talk without more subordination, shorten the pro-rata window or strengthen the flip—and accept later equity cash.

sections.callout: Your output: two complete term sheets, their modeled timing differences, and one deliberate 10 bps lever change.

flashcards.front: Which lever most directly reduces senior extension risk?
flashcards.back: An early flip to sequential pay with turboed senior principal.

flashcards.front: How does a higher OC target affect equity?
flashcards.back: It delays equity distributions until the larger target is built or restored.

flashcards.front: Why use a step-up when triggers are strict?
flashcards.back: It provides an independent carry incentive and can force sequential pay even without a breach.

flashcards.front: What do daily sweeps improve?
flashcards.back: Cash control by reducing the amount and duration of servicer commingling exposure.

flashcards.front: Why might a reserve be cheaper than more subordination?
flashcards.back: It is a targeted liquidity buffer, while extra subordination raises weighted funding cost more broadly.

quiz.q: Which change most directly delays equity?
quiz.explain: More cash must be retained to reach or restore the higher OC target before equity can be paid.

quiz.q: Which blueprint is usually more investor-friendly?
options: Tight flips, higher OC, and daily sweeps
quiz.explain: It builds protection faster and reduces both extension and cash-control risks.

quiz.q: What does PDL permission primarily protect?
quiz.explain: Principal may temporarily cover interest, with the resulting debit cured before junior principal resumes.

quiz.q: Why can a par-efficient structure price wider?
options: It leaves more extension and timing risk with seniors
quiz.explain: Lower CE and milder timing protections can require additional spread compensation.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to test a lever change?
options: Predict its effect and compare modeled outputs
quiz.explain: A controlled change connects structure, modeled mechanics, and economic trade-off.

29.title: From CSV to Excel Model: Formulas, Checks, Charts
29.prerequisite: Know the waterfall order, class interest and principal, XS, reserve top-ups, OC tests, sequential/pro-rata rules, and step-ups.
29.later: This controlled model supports the Day 30 exam review and can be adapted for warehouse and pool-management decisions in Days 31–32.

sections.label: Design
sections.title: Separate inputs, logic, and outputs
sections.lead: A clear tab structure helps reviewers distinguish assumptions from calculations and management views.

bullets.title: Inputs
bullets.text: Store fee methods, dates, toggles, OC targets, and reserve targets in one place.

bullets.title: Tape
bullets.text: Optionally hold beginning balances, coupons, and period performance assumptions separately.

bullets.title: Waterfall
bullets.text: Calculate fees, interest, XS, reserve and OC movements, principal, and equity by period.

bullets.title: Dashboard
bullets.text: Show OC path, equity on/off, class balances, and pass/fail flags without duplicating logic.

sections.callout: A dashboard should reveal the model; it should never become a second model.

sections.label: Calculate
sections.title: Implement the core formulas
sections.lead: Each formula should map to an explicit waterfall priority or structural test.

bullets.title: Fees and interest
bullets.text: Calculate monthly servicing fees and A/B interest from proxy asset or beginning note balances.

bullets.title: XS
bullets.text: Asset interest plus recoveries minus fees, swap cost, and A/B interest equals excess spread.

bullets.title: Reserve and equity
bullets.text: Top the reserve from positive XS; distribute the remainder only when required tests pass.

bullets.title: Principal
bullets.text: Sequential pay fills A first; pro-rata pay allocates by beginning class balances when permitted.

sections.callout: When OC fails, equity must be zero and non-negative residual XS should build protection.

sections.label: Control
sections.title: Add toggles and integrity checks
sections.lead: Model controls should prevent an impossible cash-flow result from looking plausible.

bullets.title: OC flag
bullets.text: Use OC ratio proxy = 1 + OC end divided by ending rated notes, then compare it with the target.

bullets.title: Mode toggle
bullets.text: Allow pro-rata only before step-up and while required tests pass; otherwise use sequential pay.

bullets.title: Cash balance
bullets.text: Require total sources minus total uses to equal zero in every period.

bullets.title: Bounds
bullets.text: Prevent negative class, reserve, OC, or PDL balances and enforce trigger consistency.

sections.callout: A red integrity check is a model failure, not an interesting scenario result.

sections.label: Explain
sections.title: Lab: Prove fail-and-cure logic
sections.lead: Using the stub's first-period intuition—A interest about 29,167, B interest 13,333, servicing 8,333, trustee fees 3,000, and XS about 51,167—run one OC fail and one cure.

bullets.title: Period 1 fail
bullets.text: Set equity to zero, apply positive XS to OC, and allocate 300,000 of sequential principal to Class A.

bullets.title: Period 2 cure
bullets.text: Once OC passes and the reserve is at target, allow residual XS to resume flowing to equity.

bullets.title: Reconcile
bullets.text: Require sources minus uses to equal zero and confirm that no class, reserve, OC, or PDL balance is negative.

bullets.title: Visualize
bullets.text: Chart the OC threshold and A/B balances, then add a traffic light for the pass-and-cure transition.

sections.callout: Your output: both OC ratios, both equity distributions, a zero cash check, and one extra traffic-light control.

flashcards.front: What is the XS formula used here?
flashcards.back: Asset interest + recoveries − servicing, trustee, swap, A interest, and B interest.

flashcards.front: When must equity equal zero?
flashcards.back: When OC or IC fails, or another post-breach rule requires cash trapping.

flashcards.front: How does pro-rata allocate principal?
flashcards.back: It splits available principal by the classes' beginning balance shares.

flashcards.front: What is the key cash integrity check?
flashcards.back: Sources minus uses must equal exactly zero in every period.

flashcards.front: What does the step-up flag do?
flashcards.back: It can end pro-rata pay and force sequential amortization after the specified date.

quiz.q: Which tab should contain fee and trigger assumptions?
quiz.explain: Centralizing assumptions in Inputs improves traceability and scenario control.

quiz.q: OC fails while XS is positive. What should the model do?
options: Trap XS toward OC and set equity to zero
quiz.explain: The failed test redirects cash to rebuild protection.

quiz.q: What proves cash conservation?
quiz.explain: Every dollar entering the waterfall must reconcile to a permitted use.

quiz.q: When is pro-rata principal permitted in the simplified model?
options: Only when the toggle, tests, and step-up conditions allow it
quiz.explain: The mode is conditional on both time and performance rules.

quiz.q: Which chart best reveals extension behavior?
quiz.explain: Class-balance paths show how quickly each note is amortizing under the selected pay mode.

30.title: Final Exam, Answers & Quick Reference
30.prerequisite: Complete the preceding legal, collateral, performance, modeling, structuring, and pricing lessons before attempting the exam without notes.
30.later: Use the results to identify weak spots before applying the course to live pool funding and encumbrance operations in Days 31–32.

sections.label: Test
sections.title: Prove the end-to-end mental model
sections.lead: The final exam checks whether you can connect legal isolation, waterfall mechanics, performance, modeling, and pricing without prompts.

bullets.title: Legal
bullets.text: Explain bankruptcy remoteness, true sale, definitive documents, and the clean-up call.

bullets.title: Structure
bullets.text: Order waterfall items and explain CE, OC, IC, PDL, triggers, and sequential pay.

bullets.title: Performance
bullets.text: Interpret delinquencies, severity, recoveries, extension risk, and EV diligence.

bullets.title: Markets
bullets.text: Estimate yield and price sensitivity, match comps by WAL, and explain prime versus subprime spreads.

sections.callout: Answer from memory first; the gap between recall and recognition is the real learning signal.

sections.label: Diagnose
sections.title: Self-grade for weak links
sections.lead: The answer key is most useful when each miss sends you back to a specific concept rather than merely changing a score.

bullets.title: Mechanics miss
bullets.text: Revisit waterfall order, OC/IC tests, XS trapping, PDL cure, and principal allocation.

bullets.title: Risk miss
bullets.text: Review delinquency roll, severity, recoveries, EV risks, and structural extension mitigants.

bullets.title: Pricing miss
bullets.text: Practice yield approximation, spread-to-Treasury, WAL matching, and comp adjustments.

bullets.title: Document miss
bullets.text: Return to the indenture or trust documents for definitive waterfall language.

sections.callout: Three weak topics create a focused review plan; twenty reread topics create avoidance.

sections.label: Keep
sections.title: Save the operating reference set
sections.lead: A compact toolkit makes the course reusable when a live deal or team question appears.

bullets.title: Core files
bullets.text: Keep the cheat sheet, deal-summary template, waterfall stub, quiz, and news tracker together.

bullets.title: Weekly update
bullets.text: Add two ratings or news items and one market-data point to the tracker.

bullets.title: Pricing snippets
bullets.text: Retain the rough yield and price-change formulas for quick reasonableness checks.

bullets.title: Trigger reminders
bullets.text: Document that OC and IC failure turns equity off and that specified triggers or step-up force sequential pay.

sections.callout: A reference is valuable when it shortens a real decision—not when it merely archives the course.

sections.label: Advance
sections.title: Lab: Run the closed-note final
sections.lead: Answer all 20 source-note questions without notes, self-grade, and route the three weakest concepts back to their course days.

bullets.title: Round 1
bullets.text: Complete the legal, waterfall, performance, pricing, counterparty, EV, and clean-up-call questions from memory.

bullets.title: Diagnose
bullets.text: Tag each miss to its source day and select exactly three weak topics for targeted review.

bullets.title: Repair
bullets.text: Review the relevant lesson and explain each missed answer aloud in one plain-English sentence.

bullets.title: Retest
bullets.text: Answer the three questions again without notes and save the quick-reference links you actually needed.

sections.callout: Your output: a score, three named weak links, and three corrected explanations you can teach to a colleague.

flashcards.front: What happens on an OC fail?
flashcards.back: Equity turns off, XS is trapped, and principal usually turboes sequentially toward seniors.

flashcards.front: Which delinquency bucket best signals near-term charge-offs?
flashcards.back: 90+ delinquency, because it is closest to charge-off and has the highest roll-to-loss probability.

flashcards.front: What is a clean-up call?
flashcards.back: An optional trust redemption once collateral falls below a stated threshold, often 10% of original balance.

flashcards.front: Where is definitive waterfall language found?
flashcards.back: In the indenture and trust documents, not merely the presale summary.

flashcards.front: What most quickly reduces senior extension risk?
flashcards.back: An early flip to sequential pay that turboes senior principal.

quiz.q: What is the most durable CE component?
quiz.explain: Junior claims provide funded first-loss protection beneath the senior class.

quiz.q: Which document is definitive for waterfall language?
quiz.explain: The governing transaction documents contain the binding priority-of-payments terms.

quiz.q: What usually happens when IC falls below 1.0x?
quiz.explain: The structure diverts cash from equity to protect note payments and rebuild support.

quiz.q: Why match WAL when comparing Treasury spreads?
quiz.explain: A maturity-matched benchmark makes spread compensation comparable across exposure periods.

quiz.q: What should you do after identifying three weak exam topics?
options: Review the relevant day files and re-test
quiz.explain: Targeted retrieval and re-testing address the specific broken links efficiently.

31.title: Funding & Pool Management: Buybox, Ramp, Covenants
31.prerequisite: Understand collateral stratifications, eligibility, performance triggers, term ABS structure, and the difference between origination and securitization decisions.
31.later: The pool's funding path leads directly to Day 32's asset-level encumbrance states and transition controls.

sections.label: Filter
sections.title: Distinguish the three gates
sections.lead: Buybox, warehouse eligibility, and term ABS eligibility answer different questions at different points in an asset's journey.

bullets.title: Buybox
bullets.text: Front-end origination limits cover score, LTV, affordability, term, vehicle, geography, and dealer tier.

bullets.title: Warehouse
bullets.text: The lender's eligibility adds document completion, title and perfection steps, concentration caps, and performance limits.

bullets.title: Term ABS
bullets.text: The transaction documents define the final securitized pool, potentially with tighter delinquency or seasoning rules.

bullets.title: Alignment
bullets.text: Term eligibility should be at least as strict as warehouse eligibility to avoid stranded assets.

sections.callout: One loan can be a valid origination and still be ineligible for a particular funding facility or term deal.

sections.label: Ramp
sections.title: Build the target pool deliberately
sections.lead: A ramp plan converts pipeline assets into a clean pool while controlling data quality and concentration drift.

bullets.title: Plan
bullets.text: Set the target size and date, then add eligible pipeline assets on a regular cadence.

bullets.title: QA
bullets.text: Deduplicate records, require core fields, test reasonable ranges, and log approved exceptions.

bullets.title: Guardrails
bullets.text: Monitor low FICO, high LTV, long terms, used share, and dealer or state concentrations.

bullets.title: Headroom
bullets.text: Track how the selected assets affect warehouse availability and the term take-out path.

sections.callout: A pool can hit its target balance and still fail if its mix breaches a disclosed concentration guardrail.

sections.label: Transition
sections.title: Control prefunding and substitution
sections.lead: Assets added or replaced after closing must preserve the eligibility and profile promised to investors.

bullets.title: Prefunding
bullets.text: Post-close additions occur within a defined period and remain subject to eligibility, size caps, and stratification drift limits.

bullets.title: Substitution
bullets.text: An ineligible asset may be repurchased or replaced within the allowed window, usually on a like-for-like basis.

bullets.title: Queue
bullets.text: Maintain pre-cleared prefunding candidates and suitable replacement assets before they are needed.

bullets.title: Evidence
bullets.text: Notify the trustee and preserve the approval and collateral-schedule trail for each movement.

sections.callout: Drift limits protect investors from receiving a materially different pool after they price the deal.

sections.label: Operate
sections.title: Lab: Build a 100 million pool
sections.lead: The target is 100.0 million: 140.0 million enters the pipeline, 110.0 million survives QA, and the plan selects 95.0 million at close plus 5.0 million of prefunding.

bullets.title: Guardrails
bullets.text: Keep Used at or below 65%, LTV above 120% at or below 12%, FICO below 620 at or below 20%, and terms of 73+ months at or below 18%.

bullets.title: Concentration
bullets.text: Keep the largest state at or below 20% and document how every prefunding add changes that measure.

bullets.title: Decision
bullets.text: If prefunding raises Used to 68%, rebalance the queue or tighten add eligibility rather than breach the disclosed limit.

bullets.title: Protocol
bullets.text: Write a 12-line checklist plus a like-for-like substitution rule and maximum permitted drift by bucket.

sections.callout: Your output: a compliant 95+5 selection, quantified drift policy, and a documented response to the 68% Used breach.

flashcards.front: What is a buybox?
flashcards.back: The originator's front-end credit and product filters for loans it is willing to make.

flashcards.front: How is warehouse eligibility different?
flashcards.back: It is the lender's funding filter, adding documentation, perfection, concentration, and performance requirements.

flashcards.front: What is a prefunding drift limit?
flashcards.back: A cap on how much post-close additions may change disclosed pool stratifications.

flashcards.front: What is a borrowing-base test?
flashcards.back: A calculation of financeable collateral after eligibility haircuts, concentration caps, and other covenants.

flashcards.front: Why use like-for-like substitution?
flashcards.back: It replaces an ineligible asset without materially changing the pool profile investors accepted.

quiz.q: Which gate is applied at origination?
quiz.explain: The buybox defines which borrower and asset profiles the originator is willing to originate.

quiz.q: Why should term eligibility be at least as strict as warehouse eligibility?
options: To avoid assets that cannot move into the term deal
quiz.explain: Misaligned filters can leave funded loans stranded outside the intended term take-out.

quiz.q: What protects against post-close pool mix changes?
quiz.explain: Drift limits cap changes to disclosed stratifications as new assets are added.

quiz.q: What can happen after a warehouse stop-funding event?
options: Collections sweep to amortize the facility
quiz.explain: Stop-funding provisions typically halt draws and redirect collections toward repayment.

quiz.q: Which is part of tape QA?
quiz.explain: Clean identifiers, complete core fields, and logged exceptions are essential to pool selection.

32.title: Multi-Multi Encumbrance: Tracking, Controls, Transitions
32.prerequisite: Understand warehouse and term funding, collateral schedules, prefunding, substitution, title transfer, and perfection evidence.
32.later: This final operating model turns the full course into a controlled asset journey from origination through warehouse funding and term securitization.

sections.label: Define
sections.title: Give every asset one state
sections.lead: Multi-multi encumbrance arises when many facilities and trusts can fund the same population of receivables over time.

bullets.title: Risk
bullets.text: A receivable can be double-pledged or sit in transit without clear title and perfection.

bullets.title: Unencumbered
bullets.text: U means the asset is owned free and clear and may be pledged or sold.

bullets.title: Pledged
bullets.text: W:X identifies a warehouse claim; T:YYYY-N identifies ownership by a specific term trust.

bullets.title: Exceptions
bullets.text: R holds a repurchase or substitution in transit, while E freezes a disputed or unreconciled asset.

sections.callout: At any instant, an asset must have exactly one authoritative encumbrance state.

sections.label: Control
sections.title: Create the evidence-backed ledger
sections.kicker: Status without proof is not control
sections.lead: A single source of truth needs immutable identity, transition history, evidence links, and blocking rules.

bullets.title: Unique ID
bullets.text: Use one immutable loan or contract identifier across originator, warehouse, custodian, and trustee systems.

bullets.title: Ledger
bullets.text: Record asset ID, current state, from and to states, effective date, evidence link, and user or process.

bullets.title: Evidence
bullets.text: Link borrowing-base and trust schedules, UCC records, assignments, releases, and trustee confirmations.

bullets.title: Blocking
bullets.text: Reject transitions with an invalid source state, missing evidence, or an overlapping W or T claim.

sections.callout: The ledger should prevent a bad movement, not merely report it the next day.

sections.label: Move
sections.title: Enforce allowed transitions
sections.lead: Asset movements require a state-machine path that preserves chain of title with no overlapping effective dates.

bullets.title: U to W
bullets.text: Add the asset to a borrowing base and record the required perfection evidence.

bullets.title: W to T
bullets.text: Obtain the warehouse release, add the trust schedule and assignment, and align the dates without overlap.

bullets.title: T through R
bullets.text: Repurchases and substitutions move from T to a time-boxed R state before any new W or T destination.

bullets.title: No direct hops
bullets.text: Trust-to-trust and warehouse-to-warehouse moves require release and an intermediate controlled state rather than overlapping claims.

sections.callout: The safe sequence is release, intermediate control, then new pledge or sale—with evidence at each step.

sections.label: Reconcile
sections.title: Lab: Audit two asset journeys
sections.lead: Asset A123 moves U on 05/01 → W:WF1 on 05/03 → released 06/10 → T:2025-A on 06/11; Asset B456 moves T:2024-B → R on 04/15 → W:WF2 on 04/18.

bullets.title: A123 evidence
bullets.text: Link borrowing-base add #447, UCC evidence, warehouse release, assignment, and the trust schedule page; verify no date overlap.

bullets.title: B456 aging
bullets.text: The three-day R period is within a five-day policy, but it still needs trustee notice and new warehouse evidence.

bullets.title: Blocking rules
bullets.text: Reject a new W/T state when another is active and reject any transition without valid source state plus evidence.

bullets.title: Escalation
bullets.text: Flag any W-and-T overlap immediately, escalate R beyond five days, and freeze every E-state movement.

sections.callout: Your output: a populated ledger, two preventive blocking rules, and a five-day R-state escalation policy.

flashcards.front: What is the one-and-only-one rule?
flashcards.back: Each asset may have only one active encumbrance state at a time.

flashcards.front: What does R mean?
flashcards.back: Repurchase or substitution pending—a temporary, time-boxed state before the next valid destination.

flashcards.front: Why can trust-to-trust not be a direct hop?
flashcards.back: The first trust's title must be released before reassignment, so the asset moves through R with no overlapping claims.

flashcards.front: What report finds double-pledges fastest?
flashcards.back: A daily diff of the internal ledger against warehouse and trustee collateral schedules.

flashcards.front: Which field anchors identity across systems?
flashcards.back: A unique, immutable Asset_ID or Contract_ID.

quiz.q: An asset appears in W:X and T:2026-A on the same effective date. What is this?
quiz.explain: Simultaneous warehouse and trust claims violate the one-active-state rule.

quiz.q: What is required for a W-to-T transition?
options: Warehouse release plus trust schedule and assignment evidence
quiz.explain: The evidence must prove both release from the old claim and valid transfer to the new trust.

quiz.q: Why is R time-boxed?
quiz.explain: Aging in transit creates uncertainty about ownership, funding, and control.

quiz.q: What should happen to an E-state asset?
options: Freeze movements until reconciliation is complete
quiz.explain: The exception state prevents further movement while root cause and evidence are resolved.

quiz.q: Which control is preventive rather than detective?
options: A blocking rule rejecting overlapping active states
quiz.explain: The system stops an invalid transition before it creates a double pledge.
